body:
India's remote-sensing programme

India has developed satellite systems for observing land resources, agriculture, oceans, urban areas and natural disasters. The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) programme became operational with the launch of IRS-1A on 17 March 1988.

Indian Earth-observation missions include several satellite families with different observation priorities. Their names are useful for identifying the type of information each mission is primarily designed to provide.

Important Indian satellite families

Satellite family or missionMain observation purposeTypical applications
ResourcesatLand and natural-resource observationAgriculture, vegetation and resource mapping
CartosatDetailed Earth-surface imagingMapping, infrastructure and urban planning
OceansatOcean-related observationsOcean colour, surface conditions, marine studies
RISATRadar-based Earth observationFlood monitoring and land observation during cloudy conditions
NISARRadar measurement of changes in Earth's surfaceLand, vegetation, water and natural-hazard monitoring

Resourcesat: land and agricultural resources

Resourcesat missions are associated with observing and mapping natural resources. Their multispectral observations support the identification of crops, vegetation, land use and other surface conditions.

Repeated images can help estimate cultivated areas, identify changes in vegetation and assess agricultural conditions. Such estimates depend on the sensor, observation period, interpretation method and supporting field information.

Cartosat: detailed mapping

Cartosat satellites are associated with cartographic and detailed Earth-surface imaging applications. Their observations support the preparation and updating of maps, the study of built-up areas and the planning of infrastructure and land use.

Detailed imagery can help identify roads, settlement patterns and changes in urban growth. However, a satellite image alone does not establish legal ownership or the precise boundaries of a land parcel; those require appropriate survey and official records.

Oceansat: ocean conditions

Oceansat missions provide observations relevant to oceans and marine resources. Their information is useful for studying ocean colour, sea-surface conditions and winds over the ocean.

EOS-06, also called Oceansat-3, was launched on 26 November 2022. Its instruments include an Ocean Colour Monitor, Sea Surface Temperature Monitor and scatterometer for ocean wind information.

Ocean colour and sea-surface temperature information can contribute to identifying potential fishing zones. A potential fishing zone is an area where ocean conditions suggest a relatively greater possibility of fish availability; it is not a guarantee of a catch at a particular location.

RISAT and radar Earth observation

Radar Imaging Satellite (RISAT) missions use radar measurements to observe the Earth. Their day-and-night capability and ability to obtain useful observations through ordinary cloud cover make them important for applications such as flood mapping and agricultural monitoring during the monsoon.

EOS-04, also known as RISAT-1A, is an Indian radar Earth-observation mission launched on 14 February 2022.

NISAR: joint radar Earth observation

NISAR stands for NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar. It is a joint mission of the United States' National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the Indian Space Research Organisation.

NISAR was launched on 30 July 2025. It uses radar measurements to study changes in land, vegetation, water, ice and surface movement. Its basic significance is the ability to repeatedly observe physical changes across the Earth using radar technology.

At the 4 November 2026 content cutoff, ISRO's spacecraft-mission list records EOS-04, EOS-06 and NISAR as operational. The mission names and launch dates are historical facts; operational status may change after this cutoff.

Applications of Earth-observation data

Agriculture and vegetation

Satellite images can be used to estimate crop area, examine changes in vegetation and identify areas requiring agricultural investigation. Observations from different seasons help distinguish cultivated land from other land-cover types.

Water resources

Remote sensing supports the mapping of reservoirs, surface water, drainage patterns and changes in water spread. Such information can assist water-resource planning and the assessment of drought or flood conditions.

Forests and environment

Repeated observations help identify changes in forest cover, damaged vegetation, land degradation and the expansion of settlements into surrounding areas.

Urban and infrastructure planning

Detailed imagery provides information about roads, buildings, settlement expansion and land-use changes. These observations become more useful when combined with GIS layers and official planning information.

Disaster monitoring

Comparing observations from before and after an event can help identify the area affected by a flood, cyclone or other disaster. Where extensive cloud cover prevents useful optical imaging, radar observations can provide valuable additional information.

Satellite observations and geographic information services

The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), an ISRO centre, provides remote-sensing data services and related applications. Its Bhuvan geospatial platform makes satellite-derived information and thematic geographical products available for different uses, including agriculture, water resources, urban planning and disaster management.

Bhuvan is a geospatial information platform, not a satellite. It helps users access and work with information obtained from satellites and other sources.

Prelims focus

  • IRS-1A was launched on 17 March 1988.
  • Resourcesat is associated with natural-resource and agricultural observations.
  • Cartosat is associated with detailed Earth-surface imaging and mapping.
  • Oceansat observations support ocean-related applications; EOS-06 is Oceansat-3.
  • RISAT and NISAR are radar Earth-observation missions.
  • Trap: Bhuvan is an information platform, not an Earth-observation satellite.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, printed pp. 92-99; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 10, printed p. 123; ISRO, Earth Observation Satellites, EOS-06 and RISAT-1 mission pages; ISRO, Spacecraft Missions, status list; NASA Science, NISAR Mission Overview; NRSC, Bhuvan Services Overview, all consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Indian Earth-Observation Satellites and Their Applications

body:
What is a meteorological satellite?

A meteorological satellite is an Earth-observation satellite designed to collect information about weather and atmospheric conditions. It can observe cloud patterns, atmospheric moisture, thermal characteristics and the development or movement of major weather systems.

Weather satellites are especially useful because atmospheric systems may cover large geographical regions and change rapidly. Repeated satellite measurements allow meteorologists to observe the development and movement of such systems.

Geostationary and polar-orbiting weather satellites

Geostationary meteorological satellites

A geostationary meteorological satellite continuously observes a large region of the Earth from approximately the same viewing position. It can repeatedly record changes in clouds and other atmospheric conditions.

This capability is important for monitoring the development and movement of cyclones over the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. Observations taken at successive times help meteorologists estimate storm location and follow changes in cloud organisation.

Polar-orbiting meteorological satellites

Polar-orbiting meteorological satellites observe different geographical regions as they move around the Earth. Their observations contribute to weather analysis and forecasting, including measurements that complement data from geostationary satellites.

The two systems serve complementary purposes. Geostationary satellites are particularly useful for frequent regional observation, whereas polar-orbiting satellites can provide repeated global coverage and additional atmospheric measurements.

How weather satellites observe atmospheric conditions

Visible-light observations

Visible-light images record sunlight reflected by clouds and the Earth's surface. They help identify cloud distribution and the visible structure of weather systems during daylight.

Ordinary visible-light images cannot provide the same cloud observations at night because reflected sunlight is absent.

Infrared observations

Infrared instruments can measure radiation emitted by the Earth and atmosphere. Thermal infrared images provide information related to cloud-top temperature and other thermal conditions.

These measurements can be made during both day and night. Very cold cloud tops often indicate high clouds and may be associated with deep convective cloud systems, but cloud-top temperature alone does not determine whether heavy rainfall will occur at a particular ground location.

Water-vapour observations

Observations in selected infrared wavelength bands provide information about atmospheric water vapour. Such measurements help meteorologists study moisture distribution and the movement of atmospheric systems.

Imagers and sounders

An imager obtains spatial observations of features such as clouds and atmospheric patterns. A sounder uses measurements at selected wavelengths to estimate atmospheric properties, including temperature and moisture at different atmospheric levels.

The distinction is one of observation purpose: imaging helps show where features occur, while sounding helps estimate atmospheric conditions through different layers.

How satellite observations contribute to forecasts

Satellite images and measurements provide important inputs to weather forecasting. Meteorologists combine these observations with ground weather stations, weather radars, ocean observations and numerical weather prediction models.

A numerical weather prediction model uses physical principles and observations to calculate possible future atmospheric conditions. Satellite measurements help describe the atmosphere at the start of forecast calculations and support the monitoring of subsequent changes.

Satellites do not independently produce every weather forecast or warning. Forecast preparation requires observation, interpretation, analysis and expert meteorological assessment.

Cyclone monitoring and early warning

Tropical cyclones are large rotating low-pressure weather systems that develop over suitably warm tropical ocean waters. They can produce strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal storm surges.

Weather satellite observations assist in:

  • Identifying the development and organisation of cloud systems over the ocean.
  • Tracking changes in the location and movement of cyclones.
  • Estimating certain storm characteristics from satellite observations.
  • Monitoring atmospheric moisture and cloud development.
  • Providing inputs to forecasting systems and warning preparation.

These observations are particularly important over ocean areas where ground-based weather instruments are relatively sparse.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) uses satellite measurements and other observations for weather analysis, forecasting and warning services. Cyclone warnings are prepared using multiple sources of evidence rather than a satellite picture alone.

Important Indian meteorological satellites

Kalpana-1

Kalpana-1 was launched on 12 September 2002 as METSAT. It was India's first dedicated meteorological satellite. It was subsequently renamed Kalpana-1. The satellite is a historical example and is no longer operational.

INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR

INSAT-3D was launched in 2013, followed by INSAT-3DR in 2016. These meteorological satellites provided capabilities for atmospheric observation and weather-related data products.

INSAT-3DS

INSAT-3DS was launched on 17 February 2024 by the GSLV-F14 mission. It is a geostationary meteorological satellite designed to support weather observation, forecasting and disaster-warning services.

Its meteorological payloads include an imager and a sounder. The satellite also carries facilities for relaying observations from weather-data collection platforms and supporting satellite-aided search-and-rescue services.

ISRO reported that INSAT-3DS began Earth imaging in March 2024. At the 4 November 2026 content cutoff, ISRO's spacecraft-mission list records INSAT-3D, INSAT-3DR and INSAT-3DS as operational. This status is specific to that cutoff and should not be assumed unchanged in later years.

Weather observation is not the same as weather prediction. A satellite measures atmospheric conditions. A forecast uses those measurements together with other observations and scientific analysis to estimate how conditions may change.

Prelims focus

  • Meteorological satellites are Earth-observation satellites used for atmospheric and weather-related measurements.
  • Geostationary satellites provide frequent observations of a large region.
  • Visible-light imaging requires sunlight; thermal infrared observations can also be made at night.
  • Kalpana-1 was launched in 2002 as India's first dedicated meteorological satellite.
  • INSAT-3DS was launched on 17 February 2024 by GSLV-F14.
  • Trap: A satellite image alone is not a complete weather forecast.

[References: NCERT, Science, Class 7, 2018-19 printing, Chapter 8, Winds, Storms and Cyclones, printed pp. 80 and 87-89; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, printed p. 89; ISRO, Kalpana-1 mission page; ISRO, INSAT-3DS Begins Imaging the Earth, 11 March 2024; ISRO, Spacecraft Missions, status list; IMD, Satellite Meteorology Services, all online sources consulted 4 November 2026.]
